summary.title: Catching Bugs Before They Land: JiTTesting's Human-on-the-Loop Approach at Full Scale
summary.idea: LLM code review misses bugs and burdens humans, so Meta generates tests that fail on a risky diff, filters false positives automatically, and only pings engineers about the likeliest real catches.
howItWorks: Overnight, a risk score picks the previous day's riskiest diffs for test generation on spare capacity.
Dodgy-diff workflow treats each change as a mutant and writes tests that distinguish it from its parent.
Intent-aware workflow infers the diff's purpose, lists risks, builds mutants for them, and writes tests to kill each.
Tests that fail on the real diff become weak catches, ranked by an LLM judge ensemble plus deterministic rules.
Engineers set criteria and review aggregate outcomes, and are contacted only when a candidate ranks highly enough.
summary.stealThis: Before your next risky merge, have an agent write a test that passes on the parent commit and fails on your diff, then only review the failures that survive a second LLM-judge pass.
summary.goDeeperIf: you're the bottleneck reviewing agent-written code and want a concrete pipeline for filtering false positives before a human looks.
summary.quote: Engineers define success criteria early, let AI execute the testing, monitor the outcomes at an aggregate level

verdict.reason: The page teaches a transferable technique, backed by production results (60% true positives, 74 serious privacy bugs caught): generate tests that tell a diff apart from its parent, keep the ones that fail on the real diff, and filter them with an LLM-judge ensemble plus deterministic rules before a human sees anything. It lacks code or a repo, and its core is test-based verification rather than review.

summary.title: 90% of my coding agent's rework came from my own work orders
summary.idea: Stricter automated review sent more agent work back for rework, and sorting the send-backs showed most came from vague work orders, so the author added a pre-handoff check on the order itself.
howItWorks: Pull the last 10 send-backs and sort each must-fix item into 'the order was silent or ambiguous' or 'the worker ignored it'.
Before handoff, a falsifier model sees only the order plus read access to the repo, and returns at most seven ranked findings.
Each finding quotes the triggering line of the order, gives a concrete breaking input, and names the section where the fix goes.
Run the falsifier twice, since the two runs overlapped on only 25 gaps; either run alone caught 56-60% of order gaps, together 71%.
Move hard rules like never printing credentials into pre-tool hooks, and split big skills into a small core with step files read on demand.
summary.stealThis: Before your next agent handoff, run a falsifier prompt twice on the written brief, asking for ranked findings with a quoted line and a concrete breaking input, and fold the fixes into the brief.
summary.goDeeperIf: you're handing work to subagents or cheaper models and burning review rounds on rework that may really come from your own briefs.
summary.quote: Reviewing harder only catches the 90% after a full round has already been spent.

verdict.reason: It teaches a concrete pre-handoff 'falsifier' pass, run twice, that turns up gaps in the work order. Each finding is ranked, quotes the triggering line and gives a breaking input. The evidence is a rework-sorting analysis (55 of 61 must-fix items came from the order) and measured catch rates, though the actual prompt isn't published and the sample is small.

summary.title: The agent ended its turn. That is not the same as done.
summary.idea: Agent loops treat the end of a turn as task completion, so unfinished work gets reported as done; a Stop hook that inspects the repository and re-runs tests blocks that.
howItWorks: A stop_check script exits 0 only if the worktree has changes, claimed files match changed files, and tests pass.
The checker re-runs the test command itself, because the agent's console output is not evidence.
Wire it as a Claude Code Stop hook that exits 2, which blocks stopping and continues the conversation.
Read the stop_hook_active flag first and let the turn end on a second block, so a broken environment cannot loop forever.
Restore protected paths like tests from the base revision before checking, so the agent cannot edit the referee.
summary.stealThis: Before your next unattended agent run, add a Stop hook that exits 2 unless git shows changes and your own test command passes when the hook runs it.
summary.goDeeperIf: you're running long unattended agent loops and want a working stop-hook script plus its known gaps (renames, new directories, deleted or skipped tests).
summary.quote: A nudge is a suggestion. A hook is a check that runs.

verdict.reason: The page teaches a concrete Claude Code Stop hook that exits 2 unless git shows a diff, claimed files match, and the checker re-runs the tests itself, with working code, a stop_hook_active loop guard, and comments that test the script and expose its gaps.

summary.title: Your AI reviewer passed the code. Who wrote its instructions?
summary.idea: An AI reviewer follows whatever instruction files a pull request changes, so attackers target AGENTS.md, skills and MCP configs. The fix is to hash those files into each verdict and require human approval for changes.
howItWorks: Each agent verdict records SHA-256 hashes of AGENTS.md, CLAUDE.md, skills, hooks, Cursor rules and MCP configs.
If any of those files change afterward, earlier verdicts stop counting and the gate refuses.
Changes to instruction files need a person's approval, backed by CODEOWNERS or signed approvals.
Changed instruction files must be plain Markdown; images, HTML, comments and invisible characters are refused.
The policy is read from the base branch, so a PR cannot loosen the rules it is judged by.
summary.stealThis: Before your next merge of an agent-config change, add CODEOWNERS entries for AGENTS.md, skills and MCP configs so a human must approve any edit to what the reviewer is told.
summary.goDeeperIf: you're letting AI agents review pull requests and haven't considered that the PR can rewrite the reviewer's own instructions.
summary.quote: If a pull request changes AGENTS.md, and an agent reviews that pull request, whose instructions is it following?

verdict.reason: It teaches transferable guardrails for AI code review: bind verdicts to hashes of instruction files, require CODEOWNERS approval for AGENTS.md, skill and MCP config changes, refuse hidden content, and read policy from the base branch; a public demo repo shows five attacks caught, though the post is partly a release note for the author's open-source tool.

summary.title: The Agent Wrote the Code and the Tests. How Do You Know They Are Right?
summary.idea: When an agent writes both code and tests, they can share the same wrong interpretation, so check tests against independently set expected results and confirm they fail on a deliberately wrong implementation.
howItWorks: Work out a few expected results by hand from the accepted rule, before looking at the implementation.
Read each assertion: it should check the claimed value, not just a successful HTTP 200 response.
On a disposable branch, plant a small realistic bug and confirm the relevant test fails for the right reason.
Keep a contract or integration check against the real consumer where a mock could hide a mismatch.
Give a QA agent the accepted requirement and examples, not the implementer's explanation, and have a person approve any changed expectations.
summary.stealThis: Before accepting agent-written tests for your next rule-heavy change, ask the agent to show the accepted expected result, the check that establishes it, and a deliberately wrong implementation that the check rejects.
summary.goDeeperIf: you're reviewing agent-written tests and want a concrete checklist for judging whether they prove the right behavior.
summary.quote: A test suite may run successfully while proving a rule nobody agreed to build.

verdict.reason: Teaches a concrete, copyable check for agent-written tests: derive expected values independently from the accepted rule, plant a controlled wrong implementation to confirm the test fails, and feed a QA agent the requirement rather than the implementer's explanation. It has a worked pricing example but no repo or before/after evidence, and the card accurately reflects the page.

summary.title: Running AI Coding Agents in Production: My 2026 Stack
summary.idea: Agents that run unattended can leak keys and overspend, so the author wraps them in plumbing: gateway routing, runtime credential injection, narrowly scoped MCP servers, and a private network.
howItWorks: Route all model calls through a gateway so agents never hold provider keys, giving one kill switch and an auditable bill.
Keep secrets in a password manager and inject them at runtime through a local broker with output scrubbing, not a repo .env.
Use short-lived, rotating keys scoped to one service each, so a leak only affects one tool.
Give agents scoped MCP servers for filesystem, git and search, instead of prompting them to be careful.
Put agent access to infrastructure on a private tailnet and use file locks and job ownership markers to stop runs colliding.
summary.stealThis: Before your next unattended agent run, move its provider key behind a gateway or runtime-injected secret scoped to one service, so a leaked key can be revoked without breaking anything else.
summary.goDeeperIf: you're running agents unattended or on schedules and want a concrete example of credential handling, gateways, and what still breaks.
summary.quote: a well-scoped MCP server beats a prompt telling the agent to "be careful" every time.

verdict.reason: A genuine walkthrough of a production agent setup that teaches transferable patterns: gateway-held provider keys, runtime secret injection with scrubbing, single-service scoped keys and narrowly scoped MCP servers. It stays thin, though, with no configs or code and affiliate-linked tool mentions that edge toward a round-up.

summary.title: gstack plan-ceo-review SKILL.md
summary.idea: Agent plan reviews drift into silent scope changes and unrecorded approvals; this skill structures the review as a gated flow with a decision ledger, explicit mode selection, and per-change approval.
howItWorks: Pre-review audit reads git history, TODOs, CLAUDE.md and any design doc before the agent forms opinions.
Reviewer picks one of four modes (expansion, selective expansion, hold, reduction); choosing a mode approves no changes.
Every scope change is a separate ledger row with options, effort and risk, and the agent stops for an actual answer.
A fresh subagent reviews the plan and summary on five dimensions, capped at three launches.
An exit gate blocks completion until the plan ends with a verified review report and no unresolved decisions.
summary.stealThis: Before your next agent-driven plan review, keep a decision ledger where each proposed scope change is its own row and nothing counts as approved until you answer that exact question.
summary.goDeeperIf: you're building long skill files for planning or review agents and want a working example of gated approvals, state tracking and exit checks.
summary.quote: Selecting a mode does not approve changes.

verdict.reason: The actual SKILL.md teaches transferable gating patterns: a decision ledger where each scope change gets its own row and waits for an explicit answer, mode selection that approves nothing, a fresh-context reviewer subagent capped at three launches, and a blocking exit gate on the report's final line. It is dense, tied to gstack binaries, and has no before/after evidence, which keeps it at 7.

summary.title: agent-loop: a portable harness with shared instructions, skills and a nightly Dream learning loop
summary.idea: Agent lessons get lost between sessions and between tools; this repo gives Codex and Claude Code one set of instructions and skills, plus a nightly review that promotes confirmed lessons into durable instructions.
howItWorks: One installer points both Codex and Claude Code at the same instructions and eight reviewed skills, with dry-run, backups and a doctor check.
Personal context stays in a separate notes vault that the agents reference, so the repo stays generic and nothing private is copied in.
A nightly Dream run reads both agents' transcripts and git activity across repos and worktrees, then writes a digest and drafts candidate lessons.
Drafts are marked ready only when later evidence confirms them; a dream-review step walks the user through promoting each one.
Later Dream runs check whether each promoted lesson is actually holding, and follow up on earlier recommendations.
summary.stealThis: Next time you notice correcting your agent for the same mistake twice, log it as a draft lesson and only promote it to your shared instructions file once a later session confirms it.
summary.goDeeperIf: you're running more than one coding agent and want a worked example of shared instructions plus a memory loop that promotes lessons with evidence.
summary.quote: A nightly Dream review reads both agents' sessions and turns confirmed lessons into durable instructions.

verdict.reason: The card accurately describes a working repo with a concrete technique: evidence-gated lesson promotion, where a nightly review drafts lessons from transcripts and git activity, promotes them only once later sessions confirm them, then checks they hold. It loses points because the README shows the loop's design but no before-and-after evidence.
